deep.reconstruction:
The page has no running derivation. It is a set of lattice-point (dot-grid) drawings with short number columns and a few Gaussian-integer jottings. My reading is as follows; the interpretation is mine and is meant as a hypothesis.

(A) Upside-down jottings, top centre. These are Gaussian integers: 8+11i (signs garbled as -8-11), 19+3i (or -19-3i), 11+3i (most likely 3+11i), and 1+2i written twice. Assuming the readings 8+11i, 19+3i and 3+11i (my reconstruction), each is divisible by 1+2i:
- (8+11i)/(1+2i) = 6-i
- (19+3i)/(1+2i) = 5-7i
- (3+11i)/(1+2i) = 5+i

The norms are 185 = 5*37, 370 = 2*5*37 and 130 = 2*5*13. So Gauss is testing or extracting the Gaussian prime factor 1+2i of norm 5.

The top-left scraps ('17 19 / 10 11', '13.19') may be a small table of residues or quotients; they cannot be read reliably.

(B) Main figures. Two large tilted squares and one smaller tilted square (a 'rhombus') are drawn on the integer lattice, with lattice dots marked inside.
- A tilted square with side vector (a,b) has area a^2+b^2 = N(a+bi). Up to boundary conventions it contains N(a+bi) lattice points. It is the standard picture of a complete residue system modulo a Gaussian integer a+bi.
- The lines joining vertices to points on the opposite sides cut the square into pieces. In the right-hand square and the small rhombus the lines form a 3x3 pattern, i.e. the square spanned by a multiple of a Gaussian integer is decomposed into translates of a smaller residue square.

(C) Lower part. Several triangles are drawn on dot lattices, one vertex marked with a cross, with columns of integers beside them. Many of these columns are column counts of lattice points under a line of rational slope, i.e. floor sequences floor(k*q/p):
- '1 3 5 6 8 10 11 13' = floor(5k/3), k=1..8.
- '1 3 4 6 8 9 11' = floor(8k/5), k=1..7.
- '2 4 7 9 12' = floor(12k/5), k=1..5.
- '2 5 7 10 12 14' = floor(12k/5 + 1/2), k=1..6, i.e. a rounded rather than truncated count.
- '2 3 5 6 8 9' (if the last digit is 9) = ceiling(3k/2).
- The companion rows ('2 5 7 8 10 12', '2 3 5 7 8 10', '3 5 8 10', '3 6 8', '3 6', '1 4 6') are too uncertain in reading to identify.

So the sheet counts lattice points in triangles cut off by lines of slope q/p inside rectangles or tilted squares. Such sums Sum floor(kq/p) are exactly the sums in Gauss's third proof of quadratic reciprocity (1808). Their lattice-point interpretation is the geometric form usually attributed to Eisenstein (1844). The tilted squares on the Gaussian lattice indicate an attempt to carry the counting over to Gaussian-integer moduli, as in the theory of biquadratic residues. The previous page (on a cubic substitution) is unrelated.
errors: No outright errors can be established. Readings of the upside-down jottings are uncertain: '-8-11' is presumably 8+11i (or -8-11i), and '3i+11' is most plausibly 3+11i, since 11+3i is not divisible by 1+2i.
Some number columns ('2 5 7 8 10 12', '2 3 5 7 8 10') do not fit an obvious floor formula. These are likely misreadings or counts with different boundary conventions, not demonstrable slips.

results.what: Gaussian integers 8+11i, 19+3i, 3+11i are each divisible by 1+2i (quotients 6-i, 5-7i, 5+i)
Tilted lattice square with side vector (a,b), of area a^2+b^2, as a fundamental domain / complete residue system mod a+bi; subdivision of a larger square into translates
results.modern_name: fundamental parallelogram of the ideal (a+bi) in Z[i]; index [Z[i]:(a+bi)] = N(a+bi)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (1832, geometric representation of complex residues)

results.what: Column counts of lattice points under lines of rational slope inside triangles, e.g. floor(5k/3), floor(8k/5), floor(12k/5)
results.modern_name: lattice-point counting for Sum floor(kq/p), the geometric form of Gauss's lemma / third proof of quadratic reciprocity
results.usually_credited_to: Arithmetic sums: Gauss 1808. Lattice-point picture: Eisenstein 1844.

deep.surprise_reason: The sheet appears to show Gauss using explicit lattice-point pictures (triangles under lines, tilted Gaussian squares) for floor-sum counting. That geometric presentation is conventionally credited to Eisenstein (1844), though the underlying sums are Gauss's own (1808), and Gaussian-lattice residue squares are already in his 1832 work. The page is undated and fragmentary. It is mildly notable as evidence of geometric thinking in the Nachlass, not a new result.

the column '2 3 5 6 8 9' (reading the last digit as 9) is ceiling(3k/2)

transcription_corrections: The upside-down entries are Gaussian integers. '3i+11' should most likely read 3+11i (11i+3), since only that is divisible by 1+2i. '-8-11' is presumably 8+11i (or -8-11i).
In the lower list, '2 3 5 6 8 7' is probably '2 3 5 6 8 9' (= ceiling(3k/2)).
The '13' and '11' following the rows '1 3 5 6 8 10' and '1 3 4 6 8 9' belong to those rows as further terms: 1 3 5 6 8 10 11 13 = floor(5k/3), and 1 3 4 6 8 9 11 = floor(8k/5).
